title: How Publicists Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how publicists work: the publicist's role in managing a single client's public image, the two-way relationship with journalists, the sometimes-necessary spin and lying, crisis management and apologies, the skills needed (journalistic thinking and writing, networking, patience, thick skin), career entry without a degree via apprenticeship, how publicists are paid (retainer or campaign), pitching rules and media lead services, and famous publicity stunts like P.T. Barnum-style stunts by Jim Moran. The episode closes with listener mail, including a correction about kosher salt and a note about Seinfeld and film portrayals of publicists.
topics: no such thing as bad publicity

segments.title: Opening banter and teaser
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter and tease that publicists are professional liars, debating whether that depends on the circumstance.

segments.title: What a publicist does and the celebrity machine
segments.summary: They define a publicist as someone who typically represents a single person and maintains and promotes that person's public image. They discuss the 'no such thing as bad publicity' saying, the Billy Ray Cyrus example of spin, and the celebrity-media machine.
topics: no such thing as bad publicity

segments.title: The term 'flak' and PR vs publicist
segments.summary: They explain that 'flak' originates with early Hollywood publicist Gene Flack and is a pejorative for publicists, and distinguish a publicist (single person) from PR (companies or organizations).

segments.title: Pitching the media and two-way relationships
segments.summary: Publicists pitch story ideas to reporters, relying on press releases and personal relationships. The relationship runs both ways: journalists also call publicists for information, and scratch-my-back dynamics shape access.

segments.title: Gender in publicity and handling tough questions
segments.summary: Chuck notes many publicists are women, and Josh speculates on why. They discuss how publicists handle interviewers asking off-limits questions and prep clients, and the celebrity walkout videos.

segments.title: Skills needed: journalistic thinking, writing, and thick skin
segments.summary: The number one rule is to think like a journalist, and ideally write like one. Publicists need good people skills, patience, flexibility, tolerance for rejection, and must be on call at all hours.

segments.title: Crisis management and apologies
segments.summary: Publicists manage fallout from client mistakes, including social media gaffes and forced apologies. They cite NFL player Chris Carter's rookie symposium remarks and a reputed Elton John tennis-court stunt that was fabricated by the band's publicists.

segments.title: Careers: skipping college and apprenticeships
segments.summary: Publicists don't need a degree; the career starts with hands-on experience as an intern or assistant, doing grunt work and networking. Chuck admits he is a poor networker.

segments.title: Hiring publicists, pitch rules, and media leads
segments.summary: Sonic Bids interviews describe how publicists are paid by retainer or campaign and when to start. Penny Sansevieri's nine traits include thinking like a journalist, knowing pitch rules (no phone follow-ups), local media, and subject lines. Media lead services and HARO on Twitter are mentioned.

segments.title: Jim Moran stunts and film portrayals
segments.summary: Jim Moran is described as a master of publicity stunts, including a refrigerator sale in Alaska, a bull in a china shop, and opening a fake embassy for The Mouse That Roared. Hosts also mention publicist portrayals in Seinfeld and America's Sweethearts.
